related_questions.question: How do you know if your uterus is infected?

text_blocks.snippet: An inflamed or infected uterus, also known as endometritis, can manifest with various symptoms. Common signs include pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal bleeding or discharge, and discomfort during intercourse. More severe cases might involve fever, chills, and gastrointestinal issues. It's crucial to be aware of these symptoms and seek medical attention promptly for proper diagnosis and treatment.
snippet_highlighted_words: pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal bleeding or discharge, and discomfort during intercourse

list.snippet: Pelvic pain: This can range from a dull ache to sharp, cramping pain in the lower abdomen.
Abnormal vaginal bleeding or discharge: This may include bleeding between periods, prolonged or heavy periods, or a foul-smelling discharge.
Painful intercourse: Discomfort or pain during sexual activity can be a sign of uterine inflammation.
Fever and chills: These are more common in severe cases of infection.
Gastrointestinal disturbances: Nausea, vomiting, or constipation can also occur.
Swelling of the abdomen: This may be noticeable in some cases.
Painful urination: This can be a symptom of both urinary tract infections and uterine infections.
General discomfort or uneasiness: Some women may experience a general feeling of being unwell.

text_blocks.snippet: What to do if you suspect a uterine infection:

list.title: 1. Seek medical attention:
list.snippet: If you experience any of the above symptoms, it's crucial to consult a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.

list.title: 2. STIs:
list.snippet: Be aware that sexually transmitted infections (STIs) like chlamydia and gonorrhea can cause PID and uterine infections. If you think you may have been exposed to an STI, get tested and treated promptly.

list.title: 3. Regular screenings:
list.snippet: Regular STI screenings are important, especially for sexually active women under 24 and those with multiple partners, according to MedlinePlus.

list.title: 4. Follow your doctor's instructions:
list.snippet: If diagnosed with endometritis, follow your doctor's treatment plan, which may include antibiotics and pain relievers.

list.title: Infections:
list.snippet: Endometritis is often caused by bacterial infections, including STIs like chlamydia and gonorrhea.

list.title: Other causes:
list.snippet: Other factors like ruptured appendix, bowel infections, vaginal infections, or certain surgical procedures can also lead to uterine inflammation, according to Better Health Channel.

list.title: Prevention:
list.snippet: Practicing safe sex, getting screened for STIs, and seeking prompt treatment for any infections can help prevent uterine infections.

text_blocks.snippet: Important note: While some mild cases of PID may resolve on their own, it's not recommended to wait and see, according to Healthline. Prompt treatment is crucial to prevent complications and ensure long-term reproductive health.

related_questions.question: Can you have PID without STD?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, it is possible to have pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) without having a sexually transmitted infection (STI), though STIs are a common cause. While STIs like gonorrhea and chlamydia are frequent culprits, PID can also develop from other infections or even normal vaginal bacteria.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, it is possible to have pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) without having a sexually transmitted infection (STI)

list.title: STIs as a cause:
list.snippet: Sexually transmitted infections, such as gonorrhea and chlamydia, are a primary cause of PID because they can travel from the vagina and cervix to the upper reproductive organs.

list.title: Other infections:
list.snippet: PID can also be caused by other types of bacteria that are not sexually transmitted, like those that can cause infections after childbirth or surgery.

list.title: Normal vaginal bacteria:
list.snippet: Sometimes, the bacteria that normally live in the vagina can overgrow and cause an infection leading to PID.

text_blocks.snippet: Risk factors for PID beyond STIs:

list.snippet: Multiple sexual partners: Having multiple sexual partners increases the overall risk of exposure to various bacteria.
Douching: Douching disrupts the natural balance of bacteria in the vagina, making it more susceptible to infection.
IUD insertion: There's a small increased risk of PID in the first few weeks after IUD insertion, but this is not a common cause.
Previous PID: Having had PID before increases the risk of recurrence.
Young age: Women under 25 who are sexually active are at higher risk.

After receiving your lab test results, your provider might adjust your prescription to better match what's causing the infection.

text_blocks.snippet: Symptoms of a uterine infection may include:

list.snippet: Pelvic pain or cramping: This is typically the most prominent symptom, located in the lower abdomen or pelvis.
Vaginal discharge: This may be abnormal in color, odor, or consistency, such as yellow, green, or foul-smelling.
Fever: This can indicate a severe infection.
Pain during intercourse: This is common in infections that affect the cervix or uterus.
Bleeding between periods or after sex: This can be irregular or heavy.
Nausea and vomiting: These symptoms may accompany severe infections.
Fatigue: Feeling tired or weak is common with infections.
Chills: This can occur in some cases.
Difficulty urinating or pain during urination: This may be a sign of an infection that has spread to the bladder.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that some women may experience no symptoms or only mild symptoms of a uterine infection. If you suspect you have a uterine infection, it's crucial to seek medical attention promptly for proper diagnosis and treatment.
